items.title: There is no centrifugal force
items.claim: Swing a bucket on a string in a circle. People say a 'centrifugal force' pulls the water outward, keeping it in the bucket. Inside the rotating bucket-frame, sure. From a stationary frame, that force doesn't exist.
items.prompt: What's actually keeping the water in the spinning bucket?

options.text: Newton's first law — the water 'wants' to travel in a straight line, and the bucket bottom keeps providing a centripetal force inward that bends its path into a circle
Gravity, which spins with the bucket

items.reveal_title: Centrifugal force is a frame-dependent fiction
items.reveal:
In an inertial frame (you watching from outside), the only forces on the water are gravity (down) and the normal force from the bucket bottom (toward the centre of the circle). Combined, they cause the water to follow a circular path — the inward acceleration is v squared over r.

The 'centrifugal' force shows up only when you do physics in the rotating frame of the bucket itself. It's a fictitious force, introduced to make Newton's laws appear to work in a non-inertial frame.

The same logic applies to washing machines, planetary rotation, and amusement-park rides. Real forces always point inward (centripetal) — the apparent outward push is an artefact of trying to use Newtonian mechanics in a rotating coordinate system.
items.why: Everyday language ('the centrifugal force pulled me to the wall') conflates two different physical descriptions. Real forces have specific causes; pseudo-forces are mathematical artefacts of non-inertial frames.

items.title: A pendulum trades potential and kinetic energy with no loss — in principle
items.claim: Pull a pendulum back to angle θ, release. At the bottom of the swing, all gravitational potential energy has become kinetic. Back at the top of the other side, all the kinetic energy is potential again. In an ideal frictionless pendulum, this swap continues forever.
items.prompt: Where does the energy actually go in a real pendulum?

options.text: It is destroyed at the bottom of the swing
Friction at the pivot, air resistance, and slight inelastic deformation of the string/rod all dissipate energy as heat. The amplitude decreases exponentially with each cycle (damped oscillation)
Energy is absorbed by Earth's gravitational field

items.reveal_title: Energy is conserved; the system simply transfers it out
items.reveal:
An ideal pendulum: m g L (1 - cos θ_max) of potential energy at the highest point becomes (1/2) m v² of kinetic energy at the bottom. The two trade places once per half-cycle.

A real pendulum loses some energy each cycle to friction at the pivot, drag through the air, and tiny inelastic effects in the string. The amplitude decays as exp(-t/τ) where τ is the time constant (typically minutes to hours for a good pendulum clock).

The pendulum's period for small angles is T = 2π√(L/g), independent of mass or amplitude. This is what made pendulum clocks accurate enough to be the global timekeeping standard from 1656 (Huygens) until ~1929 (when quartz oscillators overtook them).
items.why: Conservation of energy is taught as a static law. In a real oscillator it constrains where the energy goes — but it doesn't keep it all where you want it.

items.title: Centrifugal force is not a real force
items.claim: Swing a bucket on a string in a circle. People say a 'centrifugal force' pulls the water outward, keeping it pressed to the bucket. From an inertial frame outside the swing, no such force exists. The water's path is curved by the bucket pushing it INWARD.
items.prompt: What is actually keeping the water in the bucket?

options.text: Newton's first law — the water 'wants' to fly off in a straight line tangent to the circle. The bucket bottom provides a centripetal force inward that bends the water's path into a circle. From the bucket's rotating frame, that inward force appears as a fictitious outward 'centrifugal' force

items.reveal_title: Centrifugal force is a frame artefact
items.reveal:
In an inertial (non-accelerating) reference frame, Newton's laws hold simply. Forces on the water: gravity (down) and normal force from bucket bottom (toward centre of circle). Net force is centripetal — bends the water's path.

In the bucket's rotating frame, the water appears stationary. To make Newton's laws apparently work in this non-inertial frame, you have to add fictitious forces: a centrifugal force pointing outward, equal in magnitude to the centripetal force. It explains the felt 'push' on the water against the bucket bottom.

Fictitious forces are mathematical conveniences. They are real-feeling because we live on a rotating planet — what we call 'down' includes a small centrifugal component that makes weighed objects slightly lighter at the equator than at the poles.

The Coriolis force is another fictitious force, also from rotation — and it shapes the rotation of cyclones, drift of ocean currents, and the long-range trajectories of artillery shells.
items.why: Centrifugal force is named like a real force. It's an accounting trick that appears only when you choose to do physics in a rotating frame.
